# Summary: Education in Norway
Education in Norway is organized into three main levels: elementary school (barneskole, ages 6–12), lower secondary school (ungdomsskole, grades 8–10, ages 13–16), and upper secondary school (videregående skole, grades VG1–VG3, ages 16–19). Elementary and lower secondary education are compulsory and jointly referred to as grunnskole. Students begin receiving grades in lower secondary school, which influence admission to upper secondary schools. Upper secondary education, largely public (93% attendance in 2007), offers general and vocational tracks following reforms that merged earlier separate branches into a single flexible system. Vocational studies commonly follow a 2+2 model combining two years of school-based training with two years of apprenticeship. The 2006 reform also mandated IT integration and increased mobility between study paths. Graduation rates in upper secondary were approximately 73% as of 2017.
Higher education in Norway encompasses studies beyond upper secondary school and requires a general university admissions certificate. Institutions include universities, university colleges (høgskole), and private schools, with the majority run by the state. Universities focus on theoretical subjects and professional studies, while university colleges offer a broad range of academic degrees and professional vocations, requiring accreditation for master's and PhD programs. Access to higher education is competitive, often depending on secondary school grades, with students sometimes re-sitting exams to improve eligibility. The Norwegian Agency for Quality Assurance in Education (NOKUT) oversees educational quality, and the grading scale aligns across institutions. Private higher education constitutes about 10% of enrollment. Educators vary by qualification, with preschool teachers holding bachelor's degrees, adjunct teachers a bachelor's plus pedagogy, and lecturers a master's degree plus pedagogy.
